questions.q: Which of the following is generally considered the primary/most authoritative source of International Law under Article 38(1) of the Statute of the International Court of Justice?
o: Judicial decisions only
International conventions/treaties, international custom, and general principles of law recognised by civilised nations
Only the writings of publicists
Only United Nations resolutions
questions.src: ICJ Statute Article 38(1) — lists treaties, custom, and general principles as primary sources; judicial decisions and juristic writings are subsidiary means

questions.q: The relationship between International Law and Municipal (domestic) Law is explained by two principal theories. The 'Dualist' theory holds that:
o: International Law and Municipal Law are part of the same single legal system
International Law and Municipal Law are separate, distinct legal systems, and international law requires specific incorporation/transformation to become part of domestic law
Municipal Law always overrides International Law automatically
International Law has no application to sovereign states
questions.src: Settled doctrine — Dualist theory (Triepel, Anzilotti) treats international and municipal law as separate systems requiring transformation; contrasted with Monist theory (one unified system)

questions.q: 'De facto' recognition of a State or Government, as distinguished from 'de jure' recognition, refers to:
o: Permanent, final, and formal recognition
Provisional, factual recognition that the entity exercises effective control, without a formal declaration of legal legitimacy — it may be withdrawn more easily than de jure recognition
Recognition granted only by the United Nations
A recognition that cannot ever be upgraded
questions.src: Settled international law doctrine on recognition — de facto recognition is provisional/factual (effective control), de jure is formal and generally more permanent; de facto recognition may in due course mature into de jure recognition

questions.q: Which of the following is generally considered an essential criterion for statehood under classical international law (as reflected in the Montevideo Convention 1933)?
o: UN membership alone
A permanent population, a defined territory, an effective government, and the capacity to enter into relations with other States
Recognition by a majority of existing states as the sole criterion
Possession of a seat at the International Court of Justice
questions.src: Montevideo Convention on the Rights and Duties of States 1933, Article 1 — the four classical criteria for statehood, widely cited in PIL

questions.q: 'State Succession' in international law generally refers to:
o: The election of a new head of state within the same country
The replacement of one State by another in the responsibility for the international relations of territory, typically arising from events like independence, merger, or dissolution of states
The transfer of a treaty from one international organization to another
A change of government through a coup
questions.src: Settled PIL doctrine — state succession concerns the legal consequences (for treaties, property, debts, nationality) when one state replaces another in respect of a territory

questions.q: Under the doctrine of 'State Responsibility' for international delinquencies, a State can generally be held internationally responsible when:
o: Only when its head of state personally commits an act
There is an internationally wrongful act attributable to the State (an act or omission breaching an international obligation) causing injury to another State or its nationals
Only for acts committed during declared war
Never, since states enjoy absolute immunity
questions.src: Settled PIL doctrine (reflected in the ILC Articles on State Responsibility) — international responsibility arises from an internationally wrongful act attributable to the State

questions.q: Which of the following is a recognised mode of acquiring State territory under classical international law?
o: Occupation of terra nullius (land belonging to no one), cession, prescription, accretion, and conquest/subjugation (subject to modern restrictions under the UN Charter)
Only purchase, since all other modes are illegal
Only through UN Security Council resolution
Territory cannot be acquired under international law
questions.src: Settled PIL doctrine — traditional modes of territorial acquisition include occupation, cession, prescription, accretion, and conquest; modern international law (post-UN Charter) significantly restricts acquisition by force/conquest

questions.q: 'Nationality' in international law is generally understood as:
o: A purely domestic concept with no international significance
The legal bond between an individual and a State, entitling the State to exercise diplomatic protection over the individual and imposing certain reciprocal rights and duties
A status that can never be lost or changed
Identical in meaning to 'domicile' in all respects
questions.src: Settled PIL doctrine — nationality is the legal link between individual and state, relevant for diplomatic protection, and distinct from (though related to) domicile

questions.q: 'Extradition' in international law refers to:
o: The voluntary return of a citizen to their home country for tourism
The formal process by which one State surrenders a person (accused or convicted of an offence) to another State that has jurisdiction to try or punish that person, typically governed by a treaty
The automatic transfer of all foreign nationals upon request
A process that applies only to political offences
questions.src: Settled PIL doctrine — extradition is the treaty-based (or, less commonly, reciprocity-based) surrender of a fugitive between states for prosecution or punishment

questions.q: A well-recognised exception/limitation to extradition under international law and most extradition treaties is the:
o: Rule that all offenders must always be extradited regardless of the offence
'Political offence exception' — a person accused of a purely political offence is generally not liable to be extradited
Requirement that extradition can only occur between neighbouring countries
Rule that extradition can never be refused once treaty exists
questions.src: Settled principle of extradition law — the political offence exception is a long-standing, widely recognised limitation, subject to exclusions for terrorism/violent crimes in many modern treaties

questions.q: 'Territorial Asylum' as recognised in international law refers to:
o: Protection granted by a State within its own territorial boundaries to a person fleeing persecution
Protection granted inside a foreign embassy located in another country
A right that every individual can demand as of legal entitlement from any state
Protection that automatically confers citizenship
questions.src: Settled PIL doctrine — territorial asylum is granted by a state within its own territory; distinguished from 'diplomatic/extraterritorial asylum' (granted in embassies), which is far more restricted and controversial under international law (cf. the Asylum Case, Colombia v. Peru, ICJ 1950)

questions.q: Under the law relating to diplomatic envoys, the personal inviolability of a diplomatic agent (protection from arrest or detention by the receiving State) is:
o: Not recognised under international law at all
A well-established privilege, codified in the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations 1961
Available only to ambassadors, not other diplomatic staff
Automatically waived if the diplomat commits any offence
questions.src: Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations 1961, Article 29 — personal inviolability of diplomatic agents is a cornerstone of diplomatic immunity, codifying long-standing customary international law

questions.q: Under the law of treaties, a State's 'reservation' to a multilateral treaty generally refers to:
o: A complete refusal to sign the treaty
A unilateral statement made by a State, when signing/ratifying/acceding to a treaty, purporting to exclude or modify the legal effect of certain provisions of the treaty as applied to that State
A demand that the treaty be renegotiated entirely
An amendment binding on all other parties automatically
questions.src: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties 1969, Article 2(1)(d) — defines 'reservation' as a unilateral statement excluding/modifying the legal effect of certain treaty provisions for that state

questions.q: Consent of a State to be bound by a treaty may be expressed through various modes recognised in international law, including:
o: Only by armed conquest
Signature, ratification, acceptance, approval, or accession, as may be provided in the treaty
Only oral agreement between heads of state
Consent is never required under international law
questions.src: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties 1969, Articles 11-15 — recognised modes of expressing consent to be bound include signature, ratification, acceptance, approval, and accession

questions.q: Under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the standard breadth of the 'Territorial Sea' that a coastal State may claim, measured from its baseline, is up to:
o: 3 nautical miles
12 nautical miles
24 nautical miles
200 nautical miles
questions.src: UNCLOS 1982, Article 3 — territorial sea extends up to 12 nautical miles from the baseline, within which the coastal state exercises sovereignty

questions.q: Under UNCLOS, the 'Exclusive Economic Zone' (EEZ) extends up to how many nautical miles from the baseline, within which the coastal State has sovereign rights over natural resources?
o: 12 nautical miles
24 nautical miles
200 nautical miles
350 nautical miles
questions.src: UNCLOS 1982, Article 57 — the Exclusive Economic Zone extends up to 200 nautical miles from the baseline

questions.q: The concept of 'Common Heritage of Mankind' under UNCLOS applies principally to:
o: The territorial sea of every coastal state
The deep seabed and ocean floor beyond the limits of national jurisdiction ('the Area'), and its mineral resources
Airspace over international waters
Only the Arctic region
questions.src: UNCLOS 1982, Part XI — the deep seabed beyond national jurisdiction ('the Area') and its resources are designated the Common Heritage of Mankind, to be administered for the benefit of all

questions.q: Under the Chicago Convention 1944, the 'Five Freedoms of the Air' relate to:
o: Freedoms of speech exercised on board aircraft
A set of commercial aviation rights granted by one State to another regarding the operation of international civil aircraft services (e.g., overflight, technical stops, carrying passengers/cargo)
Rights of passengers to claim compensation for delayed flights
Rights relating only to military aircraft
questions.src: Chicago Convention on International Civil Aviation 1944 and subsequent agreements — the Five Freedoms of the Air are commercial aviation traffic rights exchanged between states

questions.q: Under international law, a State generally exercises complete and exclusive sovereignty over:
o: Outer space above its territory
The airspace above its land territory and territorial waters (subject to rights of innocent passage for civil aircraft under specific agreements)
No airspace at all
Only airspace above its capital city
questions.src: Chicago Convention 1944, Article 1 — every State has complete and exclusive sovereignty over the airspace above its territory, a settled principle distinct from the freedom regime governing outer space

questions.q: Under the Outer Space Treaty 1967, outer space (including the moon and celestial bodies) is:
o: Open to national appropriation by any State that reaches it first
Not subject to national appropriation by claim of sovereignty, use, occupation, or any other means — it is to be explored and used for the benefit of all countries
The exclusive property of the country that first launched a satellite
Governed entirely by domestic law of the launching state, with no international rules
questions.src: Outer Space Treaty 1967, Article II — outer space, including celestial bodies, is not subject to national appropriation by any means

questions.q: Under the Liability Convention (relating to space objects), a launching State is generally:
o: Never liable for any damage caused by its space objects
Liable to pay compensation for damage caused by its space object on the surface of the Earth or to aircraft in flight (absolute liability), and liable based on fault for damage caused elsewhere
Only liable if the damage occurs within its own territory
Liable only if the astronaut is a citizen of the injured party's state
questions.src: Convention on International Liability for Damage Caused by Space Objects 1972 — establishes absolute liability for surface/aircraft damage, and fault-based liability for damage in outer space

questions.q: The League of Nations, established after World War I, is generally regarded as having failed primarily due to:
o: Excessive military power
Lack of universal membership (notably the absence of the USA), absence of an effective enforcement mechanism, and the unanimity requirement in its Council, among other structural weaknesses
Too much funding from member states
It was never actually established
questions.src: Settled historical/PIL account — the League's structural weaknesses (non-universal membership, weak enforcement, unanimity rule) are widely cited as contributing to its failure to prevent World War II

questions.q: Under the UN Charter, the principal organ primarily responsible for the maintenance of international peace and security, with the power to take binding decisions (including sanctions and authorization of force), is the:
o: General Assembly
Security Council
Economic and Social Council
International Court of Justice
questions.src: UN Charter, Chapter V (Articles 23-32) and Chapter VII — the Security Council has primary responsibility for international peace and security, with binding decision-making power distinct from the General Assembly's recommendatory role

questions.q: The International Court of Justice (ICJ), the principal judicial organ of the United Nations, generally has jurisdiction over contentious cases:
o: Automatically over any dispute between any two states in the world
Only where the states concerned have consented to its jurisdiction (through a special agreement, a jurisdictional clause in a treaty, or a declaration under the 'Optional Clause')
Only in disputes involving UN Security Council members
Only in criminal matters against individuals
questions.src: ICJ Statute — the ICJ's jurisdiction over contentious cases between states is fundamentally consent-based (unlike the International Criminal Court, which deals with individuals for specified international crimes)

questions.q: Which specialized agency of the United Nations is primarily concerned with international labour standards and workers' rights?
o: WHO (World Health Organization)
ILO (International Labour Organization)
UNESCO (UN Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization)
IMF (International Monetary Fund)
questions.src: UN specialized agencies — the ILO is the specialized agency dealing with international labour standards, a tripartite body (governments, employers, workers)

questions.q: In the North Sea Continental Shelf Cases (1969), the ICJ held that for a rule of customary international law to be established, the mere existence of some state practice is insufficient. What ADDITIONAL element did the Court require?
o: Approval by the UN General Assembly
Opinio juris — evidence that the practice is followed out of a sense of legal obligation, not mere convenience or convention
Ratification by at least 50 states
Publication in the UN Treaty Series
questions.src: North Sea Continental Shelf Cases (ICJ 1969) — established the dual test for custom: (1) State practice (objective element) AND (2) opinio juris (subjective element, belief the practice is legally obligatory), not just habit or convenience

questions.q: State A grants de facto recognition to a newly formed government in State B that has effective control over most of the territory, but has NOT yet granted de jure recognition. Under settled principles, this means:
o: State A has no legal relationship with State B's government whatsoever

State A acknowledges the effective control exists but withholds a formal declaration of legitimacy, and this de facto status can later mature into de jure recognition — but the two are legally distinct stages, not automatic equivalents
De facto and de jure recognition are legally identical in every respect
State B's government cannot exercise ANY governmental functions until de jure recognition is granted
questions.src: Settled principle distinguishing de facto from de jure recognition — a frequently tested nuance since students often wrongly assume de facto recognition is a lesser but otherwise equivalent form of full recognition

questions.q: State X ratifies a multilateral treaty with a valid reservation to Article 5, which State Y (another party) objects to but does not treat as precluding the treaty's entry into force between them. Under the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties 1969 framework, the effect is generally that:
o: The entire treaty becomes void between State X and State Y
Article 5 does not apply as between State X and State Y (to the extent of the reservation), but the rest of the treaty remains in force between them
State Y is now bound by Article 5 despite its objection
The reservation is automatically void since any objection defeats it
questions.src: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties 1969, Articles 20-21 — a valid reservation objected to (but not opposed to treaty entry into force) modifies the reserving provision as between the two states to the extent of the reservation, while the remainder of the treaty stays in force

questions.q: A civil aircraft registered in State A experiences engine trouble and must make an unscheduled landing in State B's territory, without prior permission, during a genuine emergency. Under the general framework distinguishing sovereignty over airspace from rules on innocent passage, this scenario is best understood as:
o: A per se violation of State B's sovereignty with no recognised exception

A situation where customary practice and specific agreements generally recognise limited emergency/distress exceptions, though State B's fundamental sovereignty over its airspace under the Chicago Convention framework is not displaced — this is a narrow, fact-specific exception, not a general right of passage
Identical to the 'innocent passage' regime that applies to ships in territorial waters, applied automatically to aircraft
Something entirely outside the scope of international air law
questions.src: Chicago Convention 1944 framework — sovereignty over airspace is exclusive (Article 1), but distress/emergency situations are treated as narrow exceptions under general principles and specific bilateral arrangements, distinct from the maritime 'innocent passage' regime (which does not have a direct equivalent for aircraft under the Chicago Convention)

questions.q: A dispute arises between two UN member states. State A wishes to bring the matter before the ICJ, but State B has not made a declaration accepting the Court's 'Optional Clause' jurisdiction under Article 36(2) of the ICJ Statute, nor is there any treaty between them conferring jurisdiction. What is the most accurate consequence?
o: The ICJ automatically has jurisdiction because both are UN members

The ICJ generally CANNOT hear the contentious case absent State B's consent through some other recognised basis (special agreement, treaty clause, or forum prorogatum) — UN membership alone does not confer compulsory jurisdiction
State A can compel State B to appear via UN Security Council resolution as of right
The dispute must automatically go to the International Criminal Court instead
questions.src: ICJ Statute — jurisdiction over contentious cases is fundamentally consent-based; mere UN membership does NOT itself confer compulsory ICJ jurisdiction over a state that has not separately consented via the Optional Clause, a treaty's jurisdictional clause, a special agreement, or forum prorogatum — a distinction commonly missed
